P00.title: Find the missing bridge
P00.prompt: A draft says: “\(n^2+n+41\) is prime for the first \(10\) nonnegative integers, so it is prime for every \(n\ge0\).”

choices.label: The table checks only a finite sample.
The base case was not checked.

P00.correctFeedback: Correct. The examples do not cover every allowed integer.
P00.wrongFeedback: Look at the move from checked cases to every integer.
P00.reveal: At \(n=41\), \(n^2+n+41=41(41+2)\), which is composite. One counterexample refutes the universal claim. A valid proof of a true universal claim would need an argument covering every allowed input.

C02.title: From error to method

stages.prompt: A proof cancels \(4\) from \(4a\equiv4b\pmod{12}\) and concludes \(a\equiv b\pmod{12}\). Which condition failed?
stages.answer: The factor \(4\) is not a unit modulo \(12\), since \(\gcd(4,12)=4\). The valid conclusion is \(a\equiv b\pmod3\).

stages.prompt: How many inputs lie in each attained fiber of \(x\mapsto4x\pmod{12}\), and how many outputs are attained?
stages.hint: Divide the modulus by \(\gcd(4,12)\) to count attained outputs.
stages.answer: Each attained output has \(\gcd(4,12)=4\) inputs. Exactly \(12/4=3\) outputs are attained: \(0,4,8\).

stages.prompt: If \(6a\equiv6b\pmod{14}\), what is the strongest congruence on \(a-b\)? Give two distinct classes modulo \(14\) with the same output.
stages.hint: First compute \(\gcd(6,14)=2\); then reduce the modulus.
stages.answer: The equivalence is \(a\equiv b\pmod7\). Classes \(1\) and \(8\) differ by \(7\), and \(6\cdot1\equiv6\cdot8\pmod{14}\). They are distinct modulo \(14\).

C02.outro: All three stages complete. Return to the theorem and explain why the reduced modulus is exact.

Q04.title: Which boundary can the line hit?
Q04.prompt: For distinct odd primes \(p,q\), the lattice proof divides a \((p-1)/2\) by \((q-1)/2\) rectangle by the line \(qx=py\). Could an interior lattice point lie on that line?

choices.label: No: coprimality would force a coordinate beyond the rectangle.
Yes: every point with equal coordinates lies on the line.

Q04.correctFeedback: Correct. Now identify which coordinate must contain the other prime.
Q04.wrongFeedback: Check what the equality forces by Euclid’s lemma.
Q04.reveal: If \(qx=py\) with \(p\) and \(q\) distinct primes, then \(p\mid x\) and \(q\mid y\). But \(0<x<p\) and \(0<y<q\), so neither is possible. Thus the two sides partition every interior lattice point, which makes the parity count exact.

R07.title: Three units, three different roles
R07.prompt: In \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\), compare \(-1\), \(1+\sqrt2\), and \(3+2\sqrt2\). Which one generates the positive-real norm-one solutions?
R07.correctFeedback: Correct. Check the norm and the positive-real condition separately.
R07.wrongFeedback: Compute the norm first, then check positivity under the chosen real embedding.
R07.reveal: The norms are \(N(-1)=1\), \(N(1+\sqrt2)=-1\), and \(N(3+2\sqrt2)=1\). The positive-real norm-one subgroup is \(\{(3+2\sqrt2)^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}\). The full norm-one group also has their negatives, so it is not infinite cyclic; \(1+\sqrt2\) is a unit of norm \(-1\).
